'''Shannon Matilda Wells Lucid''' ([[birth name|née]] '''Wells'''; born January 14, 1943) is an American [[biochemist]] and retired [[NASA astronaut]]. She has flown in space five times, including a prolonged mission aboard the Russian space station ''[[Mir]]'' in 1996, and is the only American woman to have stayed on ''Mir''. From 1996 to 2007, Lucid held the record for the longest duration spent in space by an American and by a woman. She was awarded the [[Congressional Space Medal of Honor]] in December 1996, making her the tenth person and the first woman to be accorded the honor.

Lucid is a graduate of the [[University of Oklahoma]], where she earned a [[bachelor's degree]] in chemistry in 1963, a master's degree in [[biochemistry]] in 1970, and a [[PhD]] in biochemistry in 1973. She was a laboratory technician at the [[Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation]] from 1964 to 1966, a research chemist at [[Kerr-McGee]] from 1966 to 1968, and a research associate at the Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation from 1973 to 1978.

In 1978, Lucid was recruited by NASA for [[astronaut training]] with [[NASA Astronaut Group&nbsp;8]], the first class of astronauts to include women. She flew in space five times: on [[STS-51-G]], [[STS-34]], [[STS-43]], [[STS-58]], and her mission to ''Mir'', for which Lucid traveled to the space station on {{OV|Atlantis}} with [[STS-76]] and returned six months later with [[STS-79]]. She was the [[NASA Chief Scientist]] from 2002 to 2003 and a [[capsule communicator]] (CAPCOM) at [[Christopher C. Kraft Jr. Mission Control Center|Mission Control]] for numerous [[Space Shuttle missions]], including [[STS-135]], the final mission of the [[Space Shuttle program]]. Lucid announced her retirement from NASA in 2012.

==Early life==
Shannon Matilda Wells was born in [[Shanghai]], Republic of China,<!-- DO NOT LINK, see [[MOS:GEOLINK]] for further guidance --> on January 14, 1943,{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|pp=108–109}}<ref name="JSC"/> the daughter of Joseph Oscar Wells, a [[Baptist]] missionary, and his wife Myrtle, a missionary nurse. Due to America's [[Pacific War|ongoing war]] with Japan, when she was six weeks old, the family was detained by the [[Japanese occupation of Shanghai|Japanese, who had occupied Shanghai at the time]].  The three of them were imprisoned in an [[internment camp]] but were released during a [[prisoner exchange]] later that year. They returned to the United States on the Swedish [[ocean liner]] {{MS|Gripsholm|1924|6}} and stayed in the US until the end of the war.<ref name="Begley">{{cite magazine |last=Begley |first=Sharon |author-link=Sharon Begley |date=October 7, 1996 |title=Down to Earth: After a record 188 days in space, Shannon Lucid was still standing. It was one large step for a woman, one small step for NASA's new breed of astronaut |url=http://link.galegroup.com/apps/doc/A18722411/ITOF?u=philly_free&sid=ITOF&xid=f50e1c24 |magazine=[[Newsweek]] |access-date=October 13, 2018 |via=General One File |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=The Gripsholm WWII Exchanges |first=Evelyn |last=Iritani |encyclopedia=Densho Encyclopedia |url=https://encyclopedia.densho.org/The_Gripsholm_WWII_Exchanges/#cite_note-ftnt_ref7-7 |access-date=August 26, 2022}}</ref>{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|pp=109–111}}

After the war ended, the family returned to China but decided to leave again after the [[Chinese Communist Revolution]] in 1949.<ref name="Begley" /> They moved to [[Lubbock, Texas]], and then settled in [[Bethany, Oklahoma]], the family's original hometown, where Wells graduated from [[Bethany High School]] in 1960.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|pp=109–111}} She was fascinated by stories of the [[American frontier]] and wanted to become an explorer. She concluded that she had been born too late for this, but discovered the works of [[Robert Goddard]], the American [[rocket scientist]], and decided that she could become a space explorer. Wells sold her bicycle to buy a telescope so she could look at the stars,{{sfn|Bredeson|1998|pp=11–12}} and began building her own rockets. Shortly after graduating from high school, Wells earned her [[private pilot's license]] with instrument and multi-engine ratings and bought a preowned [[Piper PA-16 Clipper]] that she used to fly her father to [[revival meeting]]s. She applied for jobs as a commercial pilot, but was rejected, as women were not yet accepted for training as commercial pilots in the United States.<ref name="Begley" />{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|pp=109–111}}{{sfn|Bredeson|1998|p=14}}

Wells attended [[Wheaton College (Illinois)|Wheaton College]] in [[Illinois]], where she majored in [[chemistry]]. She then transferred to the [[University of Oklahoma]], where she earned her [[bachelor's degree]] in chemistry in 1963. She was a teaching assistant in the University of Oklahoma's Department of Chemistry from 1963 to 1964 and a senior laboratory technician at the [[Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation]] in [[Oklahoma City]], from 1964 to 1966. She then became a research chemist at [[Kerr-McGee]], an oil company there.<ref name="Begley" />{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|pp=109–111}} At Kerr-McGee she met Michael F. Lucid, a fellow research chemist.  They married in 1967,<ref>{{cite news |title=Record-setting astronaut remains down to Earth |date=September 27, 1996 |newspaper=[[The Courier-Journal]] |location=Louisville, Kentucky |page=2 |via=Newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/116073565/shannon-lucid-profile/ |access-date=August 28, 2022 }}</ref> and their first child, Kawai Dawn, was born in 1968.<ref name="Begley" />{{sfn|Bredeson|1998|p=16}}

Afterward, Lucid left Kerr-McGee and returned to the University of Oklahoma as graduate assistant in the Department of Biochemistry and [[Molecular biology|Molecular Biology]], where she pursued a master's degree in [[biochemistry]]. She sat for her final examinations two days after the birth of her second daughter, Shandara Michelle, in 1970.<ref name="Begley" />{{sfn|Bredeson|1998|p=16}} She went on to earn her PhD in biochemistry in 1973, writing her thesis on the ''Effect of Cholera Toxin on Phosphorylation and Kinase Activity of Intestinal Epithelial Cells and Their Brush Borders'' under the supervision of A. Chadwick Cox.<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Lucid |first=Shannon Wells |year=1973 |title=Effect of Cholera Toxin on Phosphorylation and Kinase Activity of Intestinal Epithelial Cells and Their Brush Borders |degree=PhD |publisher=University of Oklahoma |hdl=11244/3683 }}</ref>{{sfn|Sokatch|2001|pp=31–32}} She then returned to the Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation as a research associate.<ref name="JSC" /> A third child, Michael Kermit, was born in 1975.{{sfn|Bredeson|1998|p=16}}

==NASA career==
===Selection and training===
{{main|NASA Astronaut Group 8}}

On July 8, 1976, the [[National Aeronautics and Space Administration]] (NASA) issued a call for applications for at least 15 pilot candidates and 15 [[mission specialist]] candidates. For the first time, new selections would be considered [[astronaut candidate]]s rather than fully-fledged [[astronaut]]s until they finished training and evaluation, which was expected to take two years.<ref name="call for applications" /> The enactment of the [[Equal Employment Opportunity Act of 1972]] reinforced the promise of the [[Civil Rights Act of 1964]] to address the persistent and entrenched [[employment discrimination]] against women, [[African Americans]] and [[minority group]]s in American society. While they had never been explicitly precluded from becoming NASA astronauts, none had ever been selected either.{{sfn|Foster|2011|pp=20–21}}{{sfn|Atkinson|Shafritz|1985|pp=134–135}} This time, minorities and women were encouraged to apply.<ref name="call for applications">{{cite press release |title=NASA to Recruit Space Shuttle Astronauts |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83128main_1976.pdf |date=July 8, 1976 |publisher=NASA |id=76-44 |access-date=September 17, 2020 |archive-date=January 15, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220115223747/https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83128main_1976.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Lucid's was one of the first of 8,079 applications received.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|p=111}}<ref name="NASA Selects 35 Astronaut Candidates" />
[[File:NASA astronaut class 1978 women.jpg|thumb|upright=1.0|left|The first NASA women astronauts. Back row, left to right: [[Kathryn Sullivan]], Shannon Lucid, [[Anna Lee Fisher|Anna Fisher]], [[Judith Resnik]]. Front row, left to right: [[Sally Ride]] and [[Rhea Seddon]].]]

As one of 208 finalists,<ref name="NASA Selects 35 Astronaut Candidates" /> Lucid was invited to come to the [[Johnson Space Center]] (JSC) in [[Houston]], Texas<!-- DO NOT LINK, see [[MOS:GEOLINK]] for further guidance -->, for a week of interviews, evaluations and examinations, commencing on August 29, 1977. She was part of the third group of twenty applicants to be interviewed, and the first one that included women. The eight women in the group included [[Rhea Seddon]], [[Anna Lee Fisher|Anna Sims]], [[Nitza Margarita Cintrón|Nitza Cintron]] and [[Millie Hughes-Fulford|Millie Hughes-Wiley]].<ref name="Third group">{{cite press release |first=Milton |last=Reim |date=August 25, 1977 |id=77-46 |title=Third Group of 20 Astronaut Applicants Includes Eight Women |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/news/releases/1975_1977/index.html#1977 |access-date=July 28, 2022 |archive-date=January 8, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230108190105/https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/news/releases/1975_1977/index.html#1977 |url-status=dead }}</ref> On January 16, 1978, NASA announced the names of the 35 successful candidates, of whom 20 were mission specialist candidates.<ref name="NASA Selects 35 Astronaut Candidates">{{cite press release |first=Milton |last=Reim |id=78-03 |date=January 16, 1978 |title=NASA Selects 35 Astronaut Candidates |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83130main_1978.pdf |access-date=July 28, 2022 |archive-date=October 10, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061010170007/http://www1.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83130main_1978.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Of the six women in this first class with female astronauts, Lucid was the only one who was a mother at the time of being selected.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Class of 1978 and the FLATs |date=November 30, 2016 |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/topics/history/features/flats.html |access-date=August 28, 2022}}</ref> [[George Abbey (NASA)|George Abbey]], the Director of Flight Crew Operations at JSC and the chairman of the selection panel,<ref name="NASA Selects 35 Astronaut Candidates" /> later stated that this was not taken into consideration during the selection process.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|pp=109–111}}

Group 8's name for itself was "TFNG". The abbreviation was deliberately ambiguous; for public purposes, it stood for "Thirty-Five New Guys", but within the group itself, it was known to stand for the military phrase, "[[Fucking New Guy|the fucking new guy]]", used to denote newcomers to a [[military unit]].{{sfn|Mullane|2007|p=63}} Much of the first eight months of their training was in the classroom.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|p=177}} Because there were so many of them, the TFNGs did not fit easily into the existing classrooms, so for classroom instruction they were split into two groups, red and blue, led by [[Rick Hauck]] and [[John Fabian]] respectively.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|p=167}} Classroom training was given on a wide variety of subjects, including an introduction to the [[Space Shuttle program]], space flight engineering, astronomy, [[orbital mechanics]], ascent and entry [[aerodynamics]] and space flight [[physiology]]. Those accustomed to military and academic environments were surprised that subjects were taught, but not tested.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|p=177}} Training in geology, a feature of the training of earlier classes, was continued, but the locations visited changed because the focus was now on observations of the Earth rather than the Moon.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|pp=165–166}}

Astronaut candidates had to complete survival training, be able to swim and [[scuba dive]], and master the basics of aviation safety, as well as the specifics of the spacecraft they would have to fly.<ref>{{cite web |title=Frequently Asked Questions |date=January 16, 2018 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/feature/frequently-asked-questions-0/ |access-date=December 30, 2022 |publisher=NASA}}</ref> Water survival training was conducted with the [[3613th Combat Crew Training Squadron]] at [[Homestead Air Force Base]] in Florida and [[parasail]] training at [[Vance Air Force Base]] in Oklahoma.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|pp=171–176}} On August 31, 1979, NASA announced that the 35 astronaut candidates had completed their training and evaluation, and were now officially astronauts, qualified for selection on space flight crews.<ref>{{cite press release |title=35 Astronaut Candidates Complete Training and Evaluation Period |id=79-53 |date=August 31, 1979 |first=Milton |last=Reim |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83131main_1979.pdf |access-date=October 3, 2020 |archive-date=October 10, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061010170330/http://www1.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83131main_1979.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Their training, which had been expected to last eighteen to twenty-four months, had been completed in fourteen. That of subsequent classes was shortened to twelve months.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|pp=190–191}}

Each of the new astronauts specialized in certain aspects of the Space Shuttle program, providing astronaut support and input. Lucid was involved with [[Spacelab 1]] crew training, and the development of the [[Shuttle Avionics Integration Laboratory]] (SAIL) at JSC and [[Rockwell International]]'s Flight Systems Laboratory (FSL) in [[Downey, California]]. She also worked on the [[Hubble Space Telescope]] and rendezvous proximity operations.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|p=199}} She was at [[Edwards Air Force Base]] as a member of the exchange crew for the landing of the [[STS-5]] mission in November 1982. The exchange crew took over from the flight crew after they had landed, and handled the post-flight activities.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|p=298}} She was an astronaut support person (ASP) at the [[Kennedy Space Center]] (KSC) for the [[STS-8]] mission in August 1983.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|p=312}} Also known as a "Cape Crusader", an ASP was an astronaut who supported vehicle and payload testing at KSC, and strapped the flight crew into their seats before takeoff.{{sfn|Collins|Ward|2021|pp=140–145}} For the [[STS-41-B]] mission in February 1984 she was the backup ASP and once again a member of the exchange crew.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|p=325}}

===STS-51-G===
{{main|STS-51-G}}

On November 17, 1983, Lucid was assigned to her first flight, the STS-51-A mission. Tentatively scheduled for October 24, 1984, the mission would be commanded by [[Daniel Brandenstein]], with pilot [[John O. Creighton]] and Lucid, Fabian and [[Steven R. Nagel]] as mission specialists. She would be the last of the six women in the TFNG group to fly.<ref>{{cite press release |first1=Dave |last1=Garrett |first2=Steve |last2=Nesbitt |id=83-046 |title=STS Flight Assignments |publisher=NASA |date=November 17, 1983 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83135main_1983.pdf |access-date=August 29, 2022 |archive-date=January 8, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230108190106/https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83135main_1983.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Due to slippages, the crew was reassigned to the STS-51-D mission in August 1984. This mission had a different payload, and it was scheduled to be launched on March 18, 1985.<ref>{{cite press release |first1=Steve |last1=Nesbitt |first2=Charles |last2=Redmond |id=84-036 |title=NASA Announces Updated Flight Crew Assignments |publisher=NASA |date=August 3, 1984 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83136main_1984.pdf |access-date=August 29, 2022 |archive-date=May 4, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210504152212/https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83136main_1984.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The mission was scrubbed just three weeks before the launch date.{{sfn|Evans|2012|pp=355–356}} In May 1985 the crew was reassigned to the [[STS-51-G]] mission. A French astronaut, [[Patrick Baudry]], and a Saudi Arabian prince, [[Sultan bin Salman Al Saud]] were assigned as [[payload specialist]]s.<ref>{{cite press release |first1=Miles |last1=Waggoner |first2=Billie |last2=Deason |id=85-019 |date=May 4, 1985 |title=ARABSAT Payload Specialist Activities |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83137main_1985.pdf |access-date=August 29, 2022 |archive-date=October 11, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061011022315/http://www1.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83137main_1985.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>
[[File:STS51G-21-005 - STS-51G - STS-51G crew activities - DPLA - adb9ddbc43bcc46aeaea54e33d29178d.jpg|thumb|On the [[STS-51-G]] mission]]

STS-51-G lifted off from [[Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39|Launch Complex 39A]] at KSC in the {{OV|Discovery|full=nolink}} on June 17, 1985. The seven-day mission was to deploy three communications satellites: <!--hide unfinished bit, https://history.nasa.gov/SP-4012/vol6/vol_vi_ch_2.pdf says telstar and morelos by Hughes but arabsat by Aérospatiale?all built by :--> [[Morelos Satellite System|Morelos I]] for Mexico, [[Arabsat-1B]] for the [[Arab League]], and [[Telstar 303]] for the United States.<ref name="STS-51-G">{{cite web |title=STS-51G |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-51G.html |access-date=August 29, 2022}}</ref> The satellites were launched on successive days during the first three days of the mission. Lucid and Fabian operated the [[Canadarm|Remote Manipulator System]] (RMS) to deploy the satellites, which were boosted into [[geostationary transfer orbit]]s by [[Payload Assist Module]] (PAM-D) booster stages.{{sfn|Evans|2012|pp=361–362}}

Lucid also used the RMS to deploy the Spartan (Shuttle Pointed Autonomous Research Tool for Astronomy) satellite, which performed 17 hours of [[X-ray astronomy]] experiments while separated from the Space Shuttle, while Fabian handled its retrieval 45 hours later.{{sfn|Evans|2012|pp=361–362}}{{sfn|Hitt|Smith|2014|pp=254–255}} In addition to the satellite deployments, the crew activated the Automated Directional Solidification Furnace (ADSF), six [[Getaway Special]]s and participated in biomedical experiments. ''Discovery'' landed at [[Edwards Air Force Base]] in California on June 24. The mission was accomplished in 112 orbits of the Earth, traveling {{convert|2.9|e6mi|e6km|order=flip|abbr=off|sp=us}} in 169 hours and 39 minutes (just over one week).<ref name="STS-51-G" />

The publicity tour that usually followed a Space Shuttle mission included a trip to Saudi Arabia. Married women were not permitted to travel to Saudi Arabia without their husband, and Michael Lucid was unavailable, so Lucid decided not to go. A devout Christian, she disapproved of the way Saudi Arabia treated women. When the rest of the crew arrived in [[Riyadh]], her absence was noted. This prompted a call from King [[Fahd of Saudi Arabia]] to President [[Ronald Reagan]]. Lucid went to Saudi Arabia and shook hands with the king, but she stayed for only one day.{{sfn|Evans|2012|pp=363–364}}<ref>{{cite news |title='A Job? But You're A Girl!': The Triumphant Career of Shannon Lucid |first=Ben |last=Evans |date=February 2, 2012 |publisher=AmericaSpace |url=https://www.americaspace.com/2012/02/02/a-job-but-youre-a-girl-the-triumphant-career-of-shannon-lucid/ |access-date=December 31, 2022 |ref=none }}</ref> For the visit to be possible, Lucid was designated by the Saudi Arabian government as an honorary man.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lucid |url=http://www.astronautix.com/l/lucid.html |access-date=2025-10-06 |website=www.astronautix.com}}</ref>

===STS-34===
{{main|STS-34}}
[[File:STS-34 crew portrait.jpg|thumb|left|The five [[STS-34]] astronauts pose for an in-space crew portrait.]]

After the STS-51-G mission, Lucid was assigned to [[Capsule Communicator]] (CAPCOM) duty. She served as the CAPCOM for the [[STS-51-J]] mission in October 1985,{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|p=344}} the [[STS-61-A]] mission in November 1985,<ref>{{cite press release |first=Terry |last=White |id=85-042 |date=October 28, 1985 |title=Mission Control Names Teams For Flight 61-A/Spacelab D-1 |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83137main_1985.pdf |access-date=August 31, 2022 |archive-date=October 11, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061011022315/http://www1.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83137main_1985.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> [[STS-61-B]] mission in November and December 1985,{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|p=345}} and the [[STS-61-C]] mission in January 1986.<ref>{{cite press release |first=Janet |last=Ross |id=85-052 |date=December 13, 1985 |title=Flight Control Of Shuttle Mission 61-C |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83137main_1985.pdf |access-date=August 31, 2022 |archive-date=October 11, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061011022315/http://www1.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83137main_1985.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The January 1986 [[Space Shuttle Challenger disaster|Space Shuttle ''Challenger'' disaster]] later that month halted Space Shuttle operations for 32 months while NASA conducted investigations and remediation. Flight crews were stood down. One consequence of the disaster was the [[Galileo project|''Galileo'' project]], an unmanned probe to Jupiter, which lost both its [[launch window]] and its ride due to the cancelation of the [[Shuttle-Centaur]] project.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|p=363}}

On November 30, 1988, NASA announced that ''Galileo'' would be deployed by the {{OV|Atlantis|full=nolink}} on the [[STS-34]] mission, which was scheduled for October 12, 1989. The mission was commanded by [[Donald E. Williams]], with pilot [[Michael J. McCulley]] and Lucid, [[Ellen S. Baker]] and [[Franklin Chang-Diaz]] as mission specialists.<ref>{{cite press release |first=Jeffrey |last=Carr |id=88-049 |date=November 30, 1988 |title=Four New Shuttle Crews Named (STS-32, STS-33, STS-34, STS-35) |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83137main_1985.pdf |access-date=August 31, 2022 |archive-date=October 11, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061011022315/http://www1.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83137main_1985.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The launch was delayed for five days due to a faulty [[Space Shuttle main engine]] controller, and then for an additional day due to bad weather. ''Atlantis'' lifted off from KSC on October 18.<ref name="STS-34" />

As the lead mission specialist, Lucid was primarily responsible for the ''Galileo'' spacecraft,<ref name="Romance of Adventure">{{cite news |title=The Romance of Adventure: STS-34 and the Voyage of Galileo |first=Ben |last=Evans |publisher=AmericaSpace |date=October 20, 2012 |url=https://www.americaspace.com/2012/10/20/the-romance-of-adventure-sts-34-and-the-voyage-of-galileo/ |access-date= January 8, 2023 |ref=none }}</ref> and initiated its deployment by pressing a button to separate ''Galileo'' from ''Atlantis''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Deployment of Galileo and the IUS |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/topics/solarsystem/features/galileo-b-20091016.html |access-date=January 8, 2023 |archive-date=January 8, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230108193230/https://www.nasa.gov/topics/solarsystem/features/galileo-b-20091016.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> ''Galileo'' was successfully deployed six and a half hours into the flight using the [[Inertial Upper Stage]] (IUS). As this was much less powerful than the Shuttle-Centaur upper stage, ''Galileo'' had to employ a [[gravity assist]] from Venus and two from Earth, and it took six years instead of two for the ''Galileo'' to reach Jupiter.<ref name="Romance of Adventure" /><ref name="STS-34" /> "Both Ellen and I sighed a great sigh of relief, because we figured Galileo was not our concern at that point, because we'd gotten rid of it," Lucid reported. "Happiness was an empty payload bay and we got happier and happier as the IUS and Galileo went further away from us."<ref>{{cite news |title='You Didn't Prepare Me': Remembering America's Galileo Mission to Jupiter, 30 Years On (Part 2) |first=Ben |last=Evans |publisher=AmericaSpace |url=https://www.americaspace.com/2019/10/27/you-didnt-prepare-me-remembering-americas-galileo-mission-to-jupiter-30-years-on-part-2/ |date=October 27, 2019 |access-date=January 8, 2023 |ref=none }}</ref>

The mission also conducted a five-day Shuttle Solar Backscatter Ultraviolet (SSBUV) experiment carried in the cargo bay, and experiments related to growth hormone crystal distribution (GHCD) and polymer morphology (PM), a sensor technology experiment (STEX), a mesoscale lightning experiment (MLE), a Shuttle Student Involvement Program (SSIP) experiment that investigated ice crystal formation in zero gravity, and a ground-based [[Air Force Maui Optical Station]] (AMOS) experiment. Lucid and Chang-Diaz operated the PM experiment, which used a laptop computer to collect two gigabytes of data from an [[infrared spectrometer]] to study the effects of microgravity on minerals. The crew filmed their activities with an [[IMAX]] camera. The mission completed 79 orbits of the Earth, traveling {{convert|2|e6mi|e6km|order=flip|abbr=off|sp=us}} in 119 hours and 39 minutes before landing at Edwards Air Force Base on October 23.<ref name="STS-34">{{cite web |title=STS-34 |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-34.html |access-date=August 30, 2022}}</ref><ref name="STS-34 Press Kit">{{cite web|url=https://historycollection.jsc.nasa.gov/JSCHistoryPortal/history/shuttle_pk/pk/Flight_031_STS-034_Press_Kit.pdf|title=STS-34 Press Kit|publisher=NASA|date=October 1989 |url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210106114019/https://historycollection.jsc.nasa.gov/JSCHistoryPortal/history/shuttle_pk/pk/Flight_031_STS-034_Press_Kit.pdf|archive-date=January 6, 2021 |access-date=January 6, 2021}}</ref>

===STS-43===
{{main|STS-43}}

In May 1990 NASA announced that Lucid was assigned to the crew of the [[STS-43]] mission, which was scheduled to be flown in ''Discovery'' in April 1991. The mission was commanded by [[John E. Blaha]], with [[Michael A. Baker]] as the pilot and Lucid, [[G. David Low]], and [[James C. Adamson]] as the mission specialists. The objective of the mission was to deploy [[TDRS-E]], a communications satellite that would form part of NASA's [[Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System]].<ref>{{cite press release |first=Jeffrey |last=Cart |date=May 24, 1990 |id=90-033 |title=Shuttle Crews Named For 1991 Missions (STS-43, STS-44, STS-45) |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83142main_1990.pdf |access-date=August 31, 2022 |archive-date=May 7, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210507115156/https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83142main_1990.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>
[[File:S43-07-010 - STS-043 - STS-43 MS Lucid conducts DTO 1208 using laptop on OV-104's flight deck - DPLA - de3eeaf53558cec138739938374e207c.jpg|thumb|Lucid conducts Development Test Objective (DTO) 1208, Space Station Cursor Control Device Evaluation{{spaces}}II and Advanced Applications, at the payload station on the aft flight deck of the {{OV|Atlantis|full=nolink}}]]

The launch date was postponed to July 23, and the orbiter was changed to ''Atlantis''. The launch was delayed by a day to replace a faulty integrated electronics assembly that controlled the separation of the orbiter and the [[external tank]], and then the countdown was halted with five hours to go due to a faulty main engine controller, and the launch was postponed to August 1. Unfavorable weather prompted yet another 24-hour delay. ''Atlantis'' lifted off on August 2.<ref name="STS-43">{{cite web |title=STS-43 |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-43.html |access-date=August 31, 2022}}</ref>
 
The crew deployed TDRS-E without incident using the IUS.<ref name="STS-43" /> The crew also conducted 32 physical, material and life science experiments, mostly related to the [[Extended Duration Orbiter]] and [[Space Station Freedom|Space Station ''Freedom'']].<ref name="JSC"/> These included experiments with the Space Station Heat Pipe Advanced Radiator Element{{spaces}}II (SHARE{{spaces}}II), the Shuttle Solar Backscatter Ultra-Violet (SSBUV) instrument, Tank Pressure Control Equipment (TPCE), and Optical Communications Through Windows (OCTW). There was also an auroral photography experiment (APE-B), a protein crystal growth experiment, testing of the bioserve / instrumentation technology associates materials dispersion apparatus (BIMDA), investigations into polymer membrane processing (IPMP), the space acceleration measurement system (SAMS), a solid surface combustion experiment (SSCE), use of the ultraviolet plume imager (UVPI); and the Air Force Maui optical site (AMOS) experiment.<ref name="STS-43 KSC">{{cite web |title=STS-43 |publisher=NASA |url=https://science.ksc.nasa.gov/shuttle/missions/sts-43/mission-sts-43.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190224031713/https://science.ksc.nasa.gov/shuttle/missions/sts-43/mission-sts-43.html |archive-date=February 24, 2019 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

''Atlantis'' performed 142 orbits of the Earth, traveling {{convert|3.7|e6mi|e6km|order=flip|abbr=off|sp=us}} in 213 hours and 21 minutes.<ref name="STS-43" /> STS-43 was the eighth mission to land at KSC, and the first one scheduled to do so since [[STS-61-C]] in January 1986.<ref name="STS-43 KSC" />

===STS-58===
{{main|STS-58}}
[[File:STS058-15-030 - STS-058 - Candid view of a crewmember in the middeck waste collection system facility. - DPLA - 530007292c4d2b753cf598fef8e4c9e7.jpg|thumb|left|Lucid, in the middeck waste collection system facility, peeking out from behind the privacy curtain]]

On December 6, 1991, Lucid was assigned to [[STS-58]], the Spacelab Life Sciences{{spaces}}2 (SLS-2) mission. This was the second mission dedicated to the study of human and animal physiology on Earth and in spaceflight. The techniques developed for this flight were intended to be precursors of those to be conducted on the Space Station ''Freedom'' and subsequent long-duration space flights. Fellow TFNG [[Rhea Seddon]] was designated as the mission [[Astronaut ranks and positions#Payload Commander|payload commander]], with [[David Wolf (astronaut)|David Wolf]], like Seddon a medical doctor, as the other mission specialist.<ref>{{cite press release |first=Barbara |last=Schwartz |date=December 6, 1991 |id=91-088 |title=Payload Crew Named For Spacelab Life Sciences-2 Mission |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83143main_1991.pdf |access-date=August 31, 2022 |archive-date=August 20, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220820031910/https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83143main_1991.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Originally scheduled as one mission, the number of Spacelab Life Sciences objectives and experiments had grown until it was split into two missions,{{sfn|Seddon|2015|pp=358–360}} the first of which, [[STS-40]]/SLS-1, was flown in June 1991.{{sfn|Shayler|Burgess|2020|pp=414–415}} The rest of the crew were not named until August 27, 1992. Blaha was designated the mission commander, with pilot [[Richard A. Searfoss]] and [[William S. McArthur Jr.]] as a fourth mission specialist.<ref>{{cite press release |first=Barbara |last=Schwartz |date=August 27, 1992 |id=92-047 |title=Crew Assignments Announced For STS-58 and STS-61 |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83144main_1992.pdf |access-date=August 31, 2022 |archive-date=December 2, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211202082154/http://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83144main_1992.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> A payload specialist, [[Martin J. Fettman]], was assigned to the mission on October 29.<ref>{{cite press release |first=Kari |last=Fluegel |date=October 29, 1992 |id=92-060 |publisher=NASA |title=Payload Specialist Selected For Second Life Sciences Mission |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83144main_1992.pdf |access-date=August 31, 2022 |archive-date=December 2, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211202082154/http://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83144main_1992.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The {{OV|Columbia|full=nolink}} with SLS-2 on board lifted off from KSC on October 18, 1993. During the fourteen-day flight the crew performed neurovestibular, cardiovascular, cardiopulmonary, metabolic and musculoskeletal medical experiments on themselves and 48 rats.<ref name="STS-58" /> The crew investigated the phenomenon of bone density loss. They also studied the effects of microgravity on their sensory perception, and the mechanism of [[space adaptation syndrome]]. To study this, on the second day of the mission Lucid and Fettman wore headsets, known as accelerometer recording units, which recorded their head movements during the day. Along with Seddon, Wolf and Fettman, Lucid collected blood and urine samples from the crew for metabolic experiments. They also drew blood from the tails of the rats to measure how weightlessness affected their [[red blood cell]] counts.<ref>{{cite web |title=STS-58 |publisher=NASA |url=https://science.ksc.nasa.gov/shuttle/missions/sts-58/mission-sts-58.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220213061656/https://science.ksc.nasa.gov/shuttle/missions/sts-58/mission-sts-58.html |archive-date=February 13, 2022 |url-status=dead }}</ref> They performed sixteen engineering tests aboard ''Columbia'' and twenty Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project experiments. The mission completed 225 orbits of the Earth, traveling five million miles in 336 hours, 13 minutes and 1 second. Landing was at Edwards Air Force Base, California.<ref name="STS-58">{{cite web |title=STS-58 |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-58.html |access-date=January 18, 2022}}</ref> On completion of this flight, Lucid had logged 838 hours and 54 minutes in space.<ref name="JSC"/>

=== Shuttle–Mir ===
{{main|Shuttle–Mir program}}
[[File:Lucid on Mir.jpg|thumb|Communicating with the ground support team inside the Core Module of ''Mir'']]

In 1992 the United States and Russia reached an agreement on cooperation in space so that Russian [[cosmonaut]]s could fly on the Space Shuttles, and American astronauts on the Russian ''[[Mir]]'' [[space station]].{{sfn|Morgan|2001|p=5}} The prospect of a long stay on ''Mir'' was not one calculated to appeal to most astronauts: they had to learn Russian and train at [[Star City, Russia|Star City]] for a year to spend several months on board ''Mir'' carrying out science experiments with Russian cosmonauts.<ref name="Legendary astronaut">{{cite news |last=Mihelich |first=Peggy |date=April 10, 2007 |title=Legendary astronaut still finds herself star-struck |url=http://www.cnn.com/2007/TECH/space/01/26/shannon.lucid.profile/index.html |access-date=September 2, 2022 |work=CNN}}</ref> "I was wondering what it would be like to spend a long period of time in space," Lucid later recalled. "I told everybody I wanted to do it, and they couldn't find anybody else who had volunteered. So they said: 'Well OK, go do it.'"<ref name="Legendary astronaut" /> In January 1995 Lucid and Blaha joined fellow astronauts [[Bonnie Dunbar]] and [[Norman Thagard]] for ''Mir'' training in Star City.{{sfn|Morgan|2001|p=11}} On March 30, 1995, NASA announced that Lucid would be the second astronaut to stay aboard ''Mir'',<ref>{{cite press release |title=For Third |first1=Mark |last1=Hess |first2=Kyle |last2=Herring |date=March 30, 1995 |id=95-39 |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/home/hqnews/1995/95-39.txt |access-date=September 1, 2022 |archive-date=October 22, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022070954/https://www.nasa.gov/home/hqnews/1995/95-39.txt |url-status=dead }}</ref> after Thagard, who arrived on the space station on March 16.{{sfn|Morgan|2001|p=23}}

Lucid's mission to ''Mir'' commenced on March 22, 1996, with liftoff from KSC aboard ''Atlantis'' on the [[STS-76]] mission. ''Atlantis'' docked with ''Mir'' on March 24, and Lucid became the first American woman to live on the station.<ref name="STS-76">{{cite web |title=STS-76 |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-76.html |access-date=September 1, 2022}}</ref> She joined cosmonauts [[Yuri Onufriyenko]] and [[Yuri Usachov]], neither of whom spoke English.{{sfn|Morgan|2001|p=45}} During the course of her stay aboard ''Mir'', Lucid performed numerous life science and physical science experiments. She lit candles to study the behavior of fire in a microgravity environment; studied the way that quail [[embryo]]s developed in their shells; grew protein crystals; and cultivated wheat in a tiny greenhouse.<ref name="Begley" />{{sfn|Bredeson|1998|p=34}} She injected herself with an immune system stimulant and collected blood and saliva samples to study the effects of microgravity on the immune system.{{sfn|Morgan|2001|p=62}}
[[File:Lucid on Treadmill in Russian Mir Space Station - GPN-2000-001034.jpg|thumb|left|Exercising on a treadmill during her stay aboard ''[[Mir]]'']]

In her free time, she read books. One novel she enjoyed immensely was ''[[The Mirror of Her Dreams]]'', however she arrived at the finish only to find it ended on a [[cliffhanger]]. "I floated there, alone in Spectra, in stunned disbelief, holding only volume one," she later recalled. "I was stranded, the impossibility of running to the local bookstore forefront in my mind{{spaces}}... How could my daughter have done this to me? Who would send only one volume of a two-volume set to her mother in space?"{{sfn|Lucid|2020|p=142}} She arranged for the second volume to be sent on the next [[Progress (spacecraft)|Progress]] resupply freighter.<ref>{{cite interview |first=Shannon |last=Lucid |interviewer-last1=Davison |interviewer-first1=Mark |interviewer-last2=Wright |interviewer-first2=Rebecca |interviewer-last3=Rollins |interviewer-first3=Paul |date=June 17, 1998 |title=Shannon W. Lucid Oral History Interviews |series=NASA Johnson Space Center Oral History Project |url=https://historycollection.jsc.nasa.gov/JSCHistoryPortal/history/oral_histories/Shuttle-Mir/LucidSW/lucid.pdf |access-date=September 1, 2022 }}</ref> She left her books on ''Mir'' for later astronaut visitors, but they became inaccessible after the [[Progress M-34]] collision in June 1997.{{sfn|Morgan|2001|p=61}} Thagard had warned Lucid about the Russians' fondness for jellied fish and [[borscht]]. She brought a supply of [[M&M's]] and [[jello]] with her, and lived on a combination of Russian and American food.{{sfn|Bredeson|1998|p=32}}

Lucid's return journey to KSC was made aboard ''Atlantis''. The [[STS-79]] mission docked with ''Mir'' on September 18, bringing Blaha as her relief, and landed back at KSC on September 26, 1996.<ref>{{cite web |title=STS-79 |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-79.html |access-date=September 2, 2022 |archive-date=May 6, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210506153032/https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-79.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> One of the catches that released her helmet from the neck ring became stuck where technicians had to use pliers and a screwdriver to remove it.<ref name="Begley" /><ref>{{cite news |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |title=Lucid Lands on Both Feet After Record-Setting Flight |first=Mike |last=Clary |date=September 27, 1996 |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-09-27-mn-48138-story.html |access-date=January 7, 2023 }}</ref> During her stay on ''Mir'', Lucid had spent nearly 400 hours exercising on a [[stationary bicycle]] and a [[treadmill]], and was able to stand and walk off ''Atlantis''. Administrator of NASA [[Daniel Goldin]] presented her with a giftwrapped box of M&M's, a gift from President [[Bill Clinton]], since she had told him that she craved them.<ref name="Begley" /><ref>{{cite interview |interviewer-last=Goldstein |interviewer-first=Edward S. |first=Shannon |last=Lucid |title=Interview: Shannon Lucid |url=https://www.nasa.gov/50th/50th_magazine/lucid.html |access-date=September 1, 2022 |archive-date=September 2, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220902013323/https://www.nasa.gov/50th/50th_magazine/lucid.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In completing this mission Lucid traveled {{convert|75.2|e6mi|e6km|order=flip|abbr=off|sp=us}} in 188 days, 4 hours, 0 minutes. This included 179 days on ''Mir''.<ref name="JSC"/> Her stay on ''Mir'' was not expected to last so long but her return was delayed twice, extending her stay by about six weeks.{{sfn|Morgan|2001|p=45}} As a result of her time aboard ''Mir'', she held the record for the most hours in orbit by a non-Russian, and most hours in orbit by a woman until June 16, 2007, when her record for longest duration spaceflight by a woman was exceeded by [[Sunita Williams]] on the [[International Space Station]].<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/sts117/news/STS-117-16.html | title = STS-117 MCC Status Report #16 | publisher = NASA | access-date = September 2, 2022 | archive-date = October 20, 2012 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121020164908/http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/sts117/news/STS-117-16.html | url-status = dead }}</ref><ref name="retires" />

===CAPCOM===
[[File:Shannon Lucid as STS-135 CAPCOM.jpg|thumb|As CAPCOM on July 12, 2011, on the [[STS-135]] mission]]

Lucid had a short cameo in the 1998 film ''[[Armageddon (1998 film)|Armageddon]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=20 facts you might not know about 'Armageddon' |first=Chris |last=Morgan |publisher= Yardbarker |url=https://www.yardbarker.com/entertainment/articles/20_facts_you_might_not_know_about_armageddon/s1__37717194#slide_2 |date=January 5, 2023 |access-date=January 8, 2023}}</ref> From 2002 to 2003, she served as [[NASA Chief Scientist|Chief Scientist of NASA]]. Starting in 2005, she served as lead CAPCOM on the Planning (overnight) shift at the [[Christopher C. Kraft Jr. Mission Control Center|Mission Control]] for sixteen [[Space Shuttle missions]], including [[STS-135]], the final mission.<ref name="JSC">{{cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/lucid_shannon_0.pdf |title=Astronaut Bio: Shannon W. Lucid (Ph.D.), NASA Astronaut (Former) |publisher=NASA|date=February 2012|access-date=April 12, 2021}}</ref> On January 31, 2012, she announced her retirement from NASA.<ref name="retires">{{cite press release |title=Legendary Astronaut Shannon Lucid Retires From NASA |first1=Joshua |last1=Buck |first2=Nicole |last2=Cloutier-Lemasters |date=January 31, 2012 |id=12-038 |publisher=NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/home/hqnews/2012/jan/HQ_12-038_Lucid_Retires.html |access-date=September 1, 2022 |archive-date=April 17, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210417202112/https://www.nasa.gov/home/hqnews/2012/jan/HQ_12-038_Lucid_Retires.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.spaceflightnow.com/news/n1201/31lucidross/|title=Breaking News – Shuttle-era astronauts Lucid and Ross retire from NASA |publisher=Spaceflight Now |date=January 31, 2012 |access-date=January 7, 2023}}</ref>

==Later life==
Lucid retired from NASA to take care of her husband Mike, who had [[dementia]]. He died on December 25, 2014.<ref>{{cite web |first= Sarah |last=Rodriguez |title=One Giant Leap for Womankind: Egalitarian Women Making History|publisher=CBE International |url=https://www.cbeinternational.org/resource/one-giant-leap-womankind-egalitarian-women-making-history/ |access-date=January 8, 2023}}</ref> She later wrote about this experience in her book ''No Sugar Added: One Family's Saga of Dementia and Caretaking'' (2019).<ref>{{cite book |title=No Sugar Added: One Family's Saga of Dementia and Caretaking |isbn=978-0578495415 |author1=Lucid |last2=Lucid |first2=Shannon Wells |date=May 6, 2019 |publisher=Shannon }}</ref> She wrote about her experiences on ''Mir'' in ''Tumbleweed: Six Months Living on Mir'' (2020).<ref>{{cite book |title=Tumbleweed: Six Months Living on Mir |isbn=978-0578671093 |last1=Lucid |first1=Shannon |date=June 13, 2020 |publisher=Shannon Jones }}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Lucid was awarded the [[Congressional Space Medal of Honor]] in December 1996 (for her mission to ''Mir''), making her the tenth person and first woman to be given this honor.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.baynews9.com/content/news/baynews9/news/article.html/content/news/articles/cfn/2014/2/7/astronaut_halloffame.html|title=Astronaut Hall of Fame adds Shannon Lucid, Jerry Ross in 2014 |publisher=Bay News 9 |access-date=January 8, 2023}}</ref> She was also awarded the [[NASA Space Flight Medal]] in 1985, 1989 (twice), 1991, 1993 and 1996; the [[NASA Exceptional Service Medal]] in 1988, 1990, 1992 and 2003 (twice); and the [[NASA Distinguished Service Medal]] in 1994 and 1997.<ref>{{cite web |title=Historical Recipient List |publisher=NASA |url=https://searchpub.nssc.nasa.gov/servlet/sm.web.Fetch/Agency_Awards_Historical_Recipient_List.pdf?rhid=1000&did=2120817&type=released |access-date=April 24, 2021}}</ref> Shanon was also awarded in Russia with [[Order of Friendship]] in 1996<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.kremlin.ru/acts/bank/10436 |title=Указ Президента Российской Федерации от 26 декабря 1996 года № 1774 «О награждении орденом Дружбы Шеннон Люсид» |access-date=2018-09-20 |archive-date=2018-09-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180920195519/http://www.kremlin.ru/acts/bank/10436 |url-status=live }}</ref> and with [[Medal "For Merit in Space Exploration"]] in 2011<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://news.kremlin.ru/media/events/files/41d36902b985e69bfeb8.pdf |title=Указ Президента Российской Федерации от 12 апреля 2011 года № 437 «О награждении медалью "За заслуги в освоении космоса" иностранных граждан» |access-date=2011-04-12 |archive-date=2012-02-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120210003253/http://news.kremlin.ru/media/events/files/41d36902b985e69bfeb8.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>. She was inducted into the [[International Space Hall of Fame]] in 1990,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/29964813/el_paso_times/|title=Slayton to Join Space Hall of Fame|newspaper=El Paso Times|location=El Paso, Texas|date=September 27, 1990|page=9|via=Newspapers.com|last1=Sheppard|first1=David |access-date=January 8, 2023}}</ref> the [[Oklahoma Women's Hall of Fame]] in 1993,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ok.gov/opm/Status_of_Women/Local%20Publish/html/hall_of_fame.html |publisher=Oklahoma Commission on the Status of Women |title=Oklahoma Women's Hall of Fame |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080906090514/http://www.ok.gov/opm/Status_of_Women/Local%20Publish/html/hall_of_fame.html |archive-date=September 6, 2008 }}</ref> the [[National Women's Hall of Fame]] in 1998,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.womenofthehall.org/inductee/shannon-w-lucid/ |publisher=National Women's Hall of Fame |title=Shannon W. Lucid |access-date=January 8, 2023 }}</ref> and the [[United States Astronaut Hall of Fame]] in 2014.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.myfoxorlando.com/story/25422720/nasa-inducts-shannon-lucid-and-jerry-ross-into-the-us-astronaut-hall-of-fame |title=NASA inducts Shannon Lucid and Jerry Ross into the U.S. Astronaut – FOX 35 News Orlando |access-date=May 5, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140505175753/http://www.myfoxorlando.com/story/25422720/nasa-inducts-shannon-lucid-and-jerry-ross-into-the-us-astronaut-hall-of-fame |archive-date=May 5, 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Lucid and Ross selected for U.S. Astronaut Hall of Fame|url=http://www.spaceflightnow.com/news/n1402/07ahof/|access-date=February 8, 2014|publisher=Spaceflight Now}}</ref> In 2002 ''[[Discover (magazine)|Discover]]'' magazine recognized her as one of the fifty most important [[women in science]].<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Svitil|first1=Kathy|title=The 50 Most Important Women in Science|url=https://www.discovermagazine.com/the-sciences/the-50-most-important-women-in-science |access-date=January 9, 2023 |magazine=Discover|date=November 13, 2002}}</ref>
